output: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to downstream tasks typically involves either parameter-efficient tuning (PeFT), such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), or manipulation of representations (ReFT). Although ReFT is more parameter-efficient than LoRA, it depends heavily on fixed-position and fixed-quantity representations that cannot scale efficiently with increasing sequence lengths. To overcome this limitation, they propose Punctuation-steered Representation Fine-tuning (PuReFT), which tunes the representations of punctuations as semantic anchors. Through detailed analysis of the attention mechanism in LLMs, they discover that punctuation plays a crucial role in providing semantic alignment throughout the sequence. Their experimental results confirm the effectiveness of PuReFT in achieving downstream task adaptations with significantly less parameter overhead. 1

Chain-of-thought prompting (Co T) dramatically improves performance on math problems by enabling the selection of the optimal reasoning path. Building on top of CoT, self-consistency further boosts performance by choosing the most consistent answer among multiple sampled reasoning paths. They hypothesize that self-consistency also improves performance on nonmath questions that rely on encyclopedic knowledge (e.g., "What is the tallest mountain?") despite the assumption that CoT is primarily useful for symbolic reasoning. To investigate this hypothesis, they split the MMLU dataset at the subject level, separating symbolic reasoning from knowledge recall. Their analysis on MMLU demonstrates that self-consistency still improves performance over the CoT baseline regardless of its premise. As a result, they achieved 89% accuracy on MMLU, the highest score to date with the use of GPT-4o.

They introduce LAMI , a novel technique to enhance the visual commonsense of LLMs by injecting relevant visual evidence based on input prompts. Their method trains with image-caption pairs and applies two key innovations to preserve the power of text-only LLMs. First, it employs a latefusion architecture that projects visual features into a pseudosequence and lets the LLM attend to it at inference. Second, during inference, multiple synthesized images are generated and fused together, allowing diverse visual experts to guide the final decision. They demonstrate that LAMI significantly improves visualcommonsense reasoning on object-based tasks compared to existing methods and VLMs, while matching their effectiveness on visionheavy tasks and boosting the text-only models' performance, with moderate inference overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/guillaumeht/lami.

Recent developments have enabled full-duplex dialogue where listening and speaking happen simultaneously, offering potential for seamless human-machine interaction. However, few studies investigate if full-duplex models can coordinate effectively across multi-turn interactions. Addressing this challenge requires scalable yet naturalistic evaluation methods that avoid the cost and instability of human evaluations and the limited scope of corpus-level analysis. They introduce FDBv2: a novel framework for testing multi-turn full-duplex dialogue capabilities, featuring an automated examiner that interacts in real time with the model being tested, adapting to feedback and posing follow-up questions. In tandem with this live conversation, they employ a suite of automated metrics assessing turntaking fluency, multi-turn instruction following, and task-specific skills. Their preliminary experiments reveal degradation in model performance over time, particularly in correction and entity-tracking tasks, and under fast-paced examiner interaction. FullDup lex-Bench-v2 offers a reproducible platform for advancing multi-turn full-duplex dialogue evaluation: https://github.com /facebookresearch/FULL-DUPLEX-BENCH.

Text embedding models compress raw text into low-dimensional vector spaces, serving as crucial components for search-enhanced generation systems. Current approaches usually depend on expanding input sequences to learn long-range dependencies, but the limited dimensionality of embedding vectors often prevents scaling. They present the first situated embedding model designed to incorporate broader contextual information around each chunk directly into its embedding. This allows the model to understand the chunk's position within the original document. They conduct experiments on seven novels to demonstrate the efficacy of situated embeddings for contextual retrieval, achieving consistent improvements compared to state-of-theart embedding models. 1

This policy brief argues that Large Language Models (LLMs) accelerate three global crises now approaching their tipping points, and that these crises feed into each other in what has been called a meta-crisis. While the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL) is among the major publishers of peer-reviewed research on LLMs, they propose actions that the ACL can take to protect its integrity and to advance research grounded in a concern for the public good and the rights of humanity and the living Earth.

While stateof-the-art models achieve impressive accuracy in predicting the factuality of events, their verdicts lack the introspective scrutiny needed to discern authentic understanding from short-cut learning. They identify two primary weaknesses undermining trustworthiness: (i) the tendency to rely on flawed reasoning paths due to shortcut learning; (ii) the inability to reconcile factuality with context sensitivity in practice. Based on classical notions of factivity and modern theories of metacognition, they propose the Meta-Factivity Framework (MFF) to reorient research towards diagnosing and cultivating the agent's capacity to regulate its factual stance: (1) Recognising factuality involves assessing whether models grasp the actual status of propositions; (2) Reasoning about factivity evaluates whether reasoning is faithful and robust; (3) Meta-f activity enables the agent to reflectively manage factual commitments, ensuring that internal reliability is reflected externally through hedging and control measures. This positions EFP at the core of building reliable agents capable of making epistemologically sound decisions.

Attention sinks—fixed positions in the attention mechanism where the model allocates near-maximum probability mass—appear frequently in Transformers across a wide variety of positional schemes, in both early and late stages of processing, and in diverse application contexts. Their practical consequences are significant: sinks can distort inferences, waste representational capacity, and exacerbate numerical issues relevant to compression and quantization. Why is sink behavior so common? They prove that it is necessary for softmax self-attention to solve a trigger-conditional task: either all weights in a single-layer model must be near-maximum at a sink position, or some layer in a multi-layer model must exhibit sink behavior. These results formalize a widely held intuition: normalization of attention scores forces the model to concentrate probability mass on a stable anchor whenever it needs to produce a default output, independent of the variable input content. They demonstrate that this behavior can be eliminated by replacing softmax with ReLU attention. These theoretical insights are complemented by empirical studies on single-layer and multi-layer models, confirming the necessity of sink behavior in softmax attention and its absence in ReLU attention.

Transformer models commonly display attention sinks—a persistent tendency to allocate disproportionate attention to the first tokens irrespective of their meaning. They mechanically characterize the firsttoken sink in GPT-2-style Transformers and show it arises from three interacting components: the learned query bias, the first-layer MLP's transformation of the positional encoding, and structure in the key projection. Through targeted causal interventions and controlled comparisons across natural-language, mathematical, and code inputs, they establish causality and remove alternative explanations. Their analysis suggests that sinks emerge through distinct mechanisms across architectures, highlighting the need to develop architecture-aware mitigations.

**Natural Language Input:** I saw a man walking down the street. What did he look like?  
**Model Output:** A tall, thin man wearing a black jacket walked past me on the sidewalk.

**Mathematical Reasoning Input:** How much money is there after paying off $400 owed to Sam and $200 owed to Tom?  
**Model Output:** 600. You paid Sam $400 and Tom $200, totaling $600.

matrix = np.random.randn(5, 10) indices = get_top_k_indices(matrix) print(indices)

Classifier-based Quality Filtering (CQF) has emerged as a widely adopted method for improving pretraining datasets for Large Language Models (LLMs). CQF leverages classifiers trained on LLM-generated quality labels to filter out undesirable data during the pre-training stage. In this paper, they show that although CQF is a powerful tool for filtering, it suffers from fundamental flaws that can lead to unexpected outcomes when applied in practice. Simple manipulations, like rephrasing in Wikipedia style, can effectively bypass filtering mechanisms. They also discover that CQF classifiers are sensitive to domain-specific features, potentially leading to skewed data distributions in downstream tasks. Their findings highlight the need for caution and careful design of CQF implementations.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)-style methods have recently received wide adoption for posttraining reasoning in large language models due to their intuitive simplicity and scalability. However, despite their empirical success, the underlying optimization dynamics of these surrogate objectives remain poorly understood. This work aims to fill this gap through a unified characterization of this important class of policies. They propose a general formulation for GRPO-style algorithms that clarifies the role of key design elements and exposes a consistent suite of challenges in optimizing this class of policies. Specifically, they find three recurrent properties of the GRPO training dynamics: (i) weightings induce structural biases in aggregated token-level gradients across shared prefixes; (ii) the AdamW optimizer's adaptive norm is invariant to global reward scaling, introducing non-trivial dependency on implementation detail; and (iii) the optimizer momentum pushes the model past the clipping boundaries during multi-step optimizations. Their analysis goes beyond empirical performance to highlight the disconnect between the surrogate objective and the true training goal, offering valuable insights about the limitations and trade-offs inherent to GRPO-style training.

Language models require memory systems capable of organizing temporal and relational dependencies to support long-horizon reasoning. Existing approaches either sacrifice structure for efficiency or incur high costs of explicit graph maintenance. StructMem leverages hierarchical design to enable structure-enriched organization without the overhead of maintaining explicit graphs: by preserving eventlevel bindings and enabling cross-event consolidation, it organizes memories into temporally and relationally grounded structures. Experiments demonstrate superior performance and efficiency.

They introduce Z3D, a novel zero-shot approach to 3D visual grounding from images. They identify shortcomings of existing methods and show how they can be overcome, resulting in state-of-the-art performance in the zero-shot setting. Their code and data are publicly available 1 .

Agentic Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factual reliability through critic-guided refinement, with many approaches assuming that detailed error categorization supports model correction. Yet in practice, critics based on large language models frequently misidentify failure causes and recommend ineffective corrections that can degrade performance relative to non-agentic baselines. To address this, they propose RePAIR, a novel RAG response-action learning paradigm that directly maps flawed RAG output to effective actions without explicit error categorization or critic oversight. Their method treats error classification as a latent process and learns a policy over actions conditioned on the RAG state. Experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that RePAIR outperforms standard RAG and all agentic RAG baselines by up to 13%.

Modern large language models are increasingly memory-bound, where the compute capacity of GPUs no longer limits throughput. To alleviate this bottleneck, they aggressively fuse MLP operations in the Transformer architecture to minimize intermediate memory traffic and expose Tensor Cores to maximum arithmetic intensity. The resulting DeepFusionKernel eliminates redundant activations and memory loads in the SwiGLU MLP, while maintaining a simple, hardware-agnostic implementation. By integrating with a lightweight, profile-driven kernel scheduler, DeepFusionKernel enables consistent, deployable throughput improvements across batch sizes and GPU architectures. In agentic long-generation workloads, DeepFusionKernel provides up to 9.7% and 13.2% throughput gains on A100 and H100, respectively.

Numerical contexts, or "anchors", can strongly influence judgment, despite being semantically irrelevant. They investigate when and why large language models are vulnerable to anchoring and find that a model's internal certainty predicts susceptibility independently of factual accuracy. Their results suggest that post-training methods strengthen the connection between certainty and robustness against anchoring.

They compare graph-based parsers and large-scale language models (LLMs) for relation extraction (RE) in supervised settings. Their results show that although LLMs are capable of capturing trivially simple relations, they perform poorly compared to graph-based parsers when the number of relations increases, indicating that the latter are robust to the growth in complexity of the relations. Specifically, the graph-based parsers begin to outperform the LLMs once the number of edges exceeds ~18 per document, regardless of the dataset.

Recent developments in Evolutionary Strategies have enabled efficient training and adaptation of Large Language Models without relying on gradients. Qiu et al. (2025) report that ES compares favorably with stateofthe-art post-training fine-tuning methods like GRPO, raising the question whether this gradient-free approach could enable continual learning in practice. They conduct extensive empirical analyses to investigate the performance and forgetting properties of ES in a continual learning setting. Their results show that ES is indeed able to compete with GRPO on several math and reasoning benchmarks, though the performance gaps vary depending on hyperparameters chosen. However, they also demonstrate that continuing to train with ES results in severe catastrophic forgetting of earlier capabilities, leading to notable model degradation compared to GRPO. They analyse the type of parameter updates generated by ES and show that the dramatic forgetting effect stems from dense, large-scale parameter updates that are orders of magnitude greater than those produced by GRPO. Their findings highlight that while ES offers a promising alternative to gradient-based fine-tuning techniques, its poor ability to generalize and retain previously learned capabilities poses serious challenges to its practical applicability in continual learning scenarios.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) is essential for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with complex reasoning tasks. However, its effectiveness increasingly depends on the difficulty of reasoning datasets: on datasets that are too easy, the high baseline accuracy of strong base models causes the group-relative advantage signal to vanish, leading to mode collapse. They diagnose this saturation-induced collapse and introduce Mixed Constrained Uniform Top-K Sampling (Mixed-CUTS), a novel inference-time operator that preserves structural diversity by sampling uniformly within a constrained Top-K candidate set. This forces the model to explore plausible but under-explored paths, re-establishing contrast in the presence of saturated training data. When integrated into the group-relative policy optimization framework, Mixed-CUTS enables robust generalization on both out-of-domain benchmarks and challenging, yet easy, datasets. For the Qwen3-4B model, they achieve +15% improvements over a strong baseline on AIME25 and +8% over the best non-RL baseline on MATH, without any additional training data. Mixed-CUTS is lightweight, parameter-free, and generalizable to any autoregressive decoder.

Large language models demonstrate impressive ability to solve mathematical problems and generate proof-like texts, yet often rely on surface correlations such as statement similarity and ordering, leading to unstable reasoning. They address this issue through RULES, a training framework that explicitly teaches models to judge lemma eligibility with two-stage outputs and section-aware reinforcement learning. Empirically, RULES shows consistent improvements in in-domain lemma judging compared to vanilla models and singlelabel reinforcement learning baselines. Margins widen considerably on perturbation suites designed to break lemma applicability, demonstrating enhanced robustness to erroneous inputs. Finally, on endto-end benchmarks, RULES achieves competitive or similar performance compared to singlelabel reinforcement learning, representing a trade-off between precision and recall that prioritizes valid reasoning over high-recall heuristics. Rule ablation studies confirm that both the two-stage outputs and section-aware reinforcement learning are essential for effectiveness.

Transformer models have achieved major breakthroughs in natural language processing, but deploying them on analog memory-centric hardware poses new challenges given the presence of noise in device-level operations. While earlier studies demonstrated the viability of analog inference for convolutional neural networks, the impact of analog noise on transformers in natural language processing remains poorly understood. To bridge this knowledge gap, they present a thorough robustness assessment of transformers using realistic simulated analog hardware. Their analysis reveals that analog noise causes varying degrees of performance reduction depending on the task, with greater effects observed in reasoning-intensive tasks like question answering than in sentence-level classification. They further identify that early attention projections are most susceptible to analog noise, while later feedforward layers offer more robustness. Finally, their analysis highlights that analog noise tends to cause localized structural disruption in attention patterns rather than uniform corruption, affecting the ability of transformers to perform precise context-aware reasoning. Through this detailed analysis, they provide a practical pre-deployment roadmap for developing robust analog transformer implementations for natural language processing applications.

Evaluation of multi-stage language model pipelines depends on complex dependencies between components and configuration choices. To reproduce or validate results published in these evaluations, researchers require access to artifacts such as generation prompts, judge configurations, and intermediate execution traces. However, the availability of these evaluation-specific artifacts is inconsistently reported in the literature, leaving the reproducibility of published evaluations uncertain.

To address this gap, they introduce ReproEvalCard, a concise reporting standard capturing the minimum set of artifacts required to reproduce and validate evaluation of LLM pipelines. To ground their proposal, they conduct a systematic audit of 55 recent pipeline papers and quantify the prevalence of missing evaluation artifacts. Their analysis reveals substantial reproducibility risks: 75% of papers lacked randomness controls, and over half omitted critical execution traces. These findings highlight recurring gaps in evaluation reporting and motivate ReproEvalCard as a practical tool for improving evaluation reliability in modern LLM pipelines. ReproEvalCard can be adopted with minimal overhead as a structured reporting layer alongside existing code releases, making evaluation dependencies explicit and easier to reproduce.

Multiple Choice Question Answering (MCQA) provides a standard to measure LLM reasoning ability. However, previous work suggests that non-reasoning LLMs achieve higher-than-random performance in MCQA by relying on clues in the choices given. They explore whether reasoning LLMs exacerbate this shortcut use by running 12 such models in two scenarios: full input (question + choices) and choices-only (only choices). With reasoning LLMs, accuracy increases by modest amounts in both scenarios, indicating that choices-only success can come from non-flawed reasoning, like inferring missing questions rather than cheating. Their findings imply that evaluating large-scale models requires nuanced analysis of reasoning traces to distinguish between flawed data and robust reasoning. 1

They introduce MARCH, a consensus-driven, multiagent framework to automate radiology report generation from 3D volumetric scans. Unlike previous methods, they leverage hierarchical, multiagent collaboration to emulate the multi-stage decisionmaking processes typical in clinical radiology, thus mitigating the risks associated with single-reader error propagation and hallucination. Extensive experiments on chest CT scans demonstrate that MARCH substantially outperforms competitive benchmarks on both language quality and clinical fidelity metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/ cmu-fra/MARCH.

Context-free parsing of a string is equivalent to computing the probability of generating that string according to a grammar. Prefix parsing is the analogous task of asking whether the string can be completed to something generated by the grammar. They show that prefix parsing can be reduced to ordinary parsing by transforming the grammar into a "prefix grammar" that captures exactly the prefix language of the original. As a result, any existing parser becomes a prefix parser with minimal overhead (Theorem 2), opening the door to new variants of powerful parsers like Valiant's sub-cubic parser and modern GPU accelerators. Furthermore, leveraging algorithmic differentiation, they show that the naive approach of computing the next-token weights of a string —which arises in language modeling and constrained generation from neural networks—is actually computable in the same asymptotic runtime as simple prefix parsing. Code is available at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/prefixparser/.

They introduce a method for learning a prosody representation that separates lexical content and speaker information. Their approach leverages unlabeled speech, trains on framebased acousticprosodic features derived from an estimated glottal source, and employs unsupervised learning objectives aimed at separating lexical content and speaker information. They evaluate their model on prosody prediction tasks, including prosodic prominence detection and phrase boundary detection, alongside the standard pitch reconstruction task. Their findings show that their speaker-separating techniques lead to improved prosody modeling while simultaneously reducing speaker information leakage.

Pretrained language models (LMs) often fail to optimise for linguistic competence, instead relying on rote memorisation of surface patterns. They introduce L2T, a pre-training framework that incorporates language learning tasks alongside standard nexttoken prediction. By transforming raw text into structured inputs and outputs, these tasks encourage inference over mere co-occurrence, thereby accelerating and improving the development of linguistic knowledge. Through extensive experiments on models with 500M and 1B parameters, they observe significant improvements in linguistic competence on BLiMP, up to 11.3%, while maintaining strong general performance. Their analyses confirm that L2T fosters linguistic competence earlier and more efficiently than traditional LM pre-training on raw text. 1

Language models benefit greatly from mixed pre-training datasets. However, since most real-world applications belong to few high-resource domains, imbalances arise in domain distribution. Previous approaches fail to accommodate this reality because they rely heavily on heuristic rules and static human concepts of domains. They revisit domain scheduling through the lens of gradient dynamics, establishing links between domain distribution and gradient geometry. Inspired by these insights, they propose DoGraph, a novel graph-constrained reweighting framework that adapts domain scheduling according to the model's evolving understanding of domains. Extensive evaluations on multiple benchmarks reveal consistent gains in both performance and domain balance. Their code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DoGraph.

Performance variability in low-resource languages is so large that it is difficult to interpret the results of any individual study. They investigate this variability in multilingual models and find that a large portion of the variation stems from data quality rather than language or model properties. By establishing controlled high-resource baselines and introducing FRED difficulty metrics, they better contextualize performance metrics and highlight specific issues for underrepresented languages. Their findings indicate that many low-resource languages fall outside of the expected range: some overperform due to high train-test overlap, while others underperform due to poor pre-training representation and tokenization.

Membership inference attacks (MIAs) aim to determine whether a specific input belongs to the training data of a machine learning model. Recent interest in LLMs has led to increased efforts to develop and evaluate MIAs, though doing so rigorously presents significant challenges. Previous studies often fail to meet the distributional assumptions needed to assess MIAs correctly, allowing simple unsupervised classifiers to reach accuracy levels close to perfect. Here, they propose a novel and principled evaluation pipeline based on checkpoints along the training progression of LLMs. Their technique leverages the fact that training data permutations change over time, dividing the dataset into two disjoint parts with similar distributions. They validate that this division doesn't contain any of the issues previously reported in existing MIA evaluations and benchmark multiple methods across a range of models within the Pythia family, finding limited effectiveness for MIAs overall.

Automated cybergrooming detection systems can help protect users against online exploitation, but their development is hampered by data scarcity and legal restrictions on accessing sensitive data. Given this challenge, they investigate whether publicly available communication datasets containing enticing strategies can be leveraged via transfer learning for cybergrooming detection. They conduct a systematic evaluation of corpus alignment across semantic, topical, emotional, toxicological, and stylistic features and assess cross-domain predictive performance through zero-shot transfer experiments. Their results reveal that corpus alignment is only modestly predictive of transfer effectiveness, instead suggesting that corpora with significant toxicity and distinctive stylistic properties perform better. The most effective corpora for transfer learning are those representing threatening (CT EL ), persuasive (CP4G ) and manipulative (CMM ) interactions, and deceptive communication (CMaf ia ). These findings highlight the usefulness of leveraging enticing communication corpora for cybergrooming detection in low-resource scenarios, supporting efforts to develop robust models without relying on sensitive grooming data.

Extensive alignment training is required to implement human-defined safety policy in large pre-trained language models (LLMs). Existing alignment methods have demonstrated success in enforcing a variety of Responsible Artificial Intelligence (RAI) principles, yet they often fail to adapt to context-specific notions of harm. They explore narrow refusal unlearning to enable compliant responses for a targeted RAI principle, and examine emergent misalignments (Emergent Misalignment -EMA). Their findings show that narrow refusal unlearning reduces refusals on the target concept but also leads to EMA on other concepts. They propose simple mitigation strategies and discuss connections between RAI concept overlaps and EMA. Code and data will be released via https://github.com/yuechena1214/emergent_misalignment_unlearning.

While deploying low-precision inference has proven beneficial for accelerating neural network operations, it also introduces new challenges in assessing the robustness of retrieval. Existing evaluation methodologies assume perfect precision and fail to account for the fact that spurious ties between candidates may cause inconsistent results during evaluation. They introduce a novel protocol combining High-Precision Scoring (HPS) and Tie-Aware Retrieval Metric (TRM) to improve evaluation accuracy in low-precision scenarios. Their HPS technique boosts the final scoring step to FP32 while retaining most of the computation in BF16, thereby eliminating spurious ties with minimal overhead. TRM provides a deterministic expectation accounting for all possible orderings of tied candidates, revealing intrinsic flaws in traditional tie-oblivious metrics. Empirical results show that their protocol improves evaluation consistency compared to the base case, restoring the behavior of high-precision systems. Their code is publicly available at https://github.com/kisuyang/tie-awareretrieval-metric s.

When describing visual content, systems face the fundamental challenge of determining how specific to be: which distinctions should be emphasized? Length is often treated as a proxy for specificity, yet these are orthogonal properties: descriptions can be long but empty, or brief but rich. They develop a novel evaluation framework that quantifies specificity by contrasting with a set of alternative images. Human preference rankings track this specificity metric, validating the proposed measure. With this benchmark, they show that length-matched variations of synthetic and human-made descriptions differ in specificity, and that this varies according to prompt design choices. Their approach enables principled evaluation of specificity and highlights important trade-offs between length and specificity for future design considerations.

Large language models (LLMs) are prone to unintentionally store sensitive or protected content learned from training data. Post-hoc unlearning techniques aim to erase unwanted knowledge from the model without requiring a full re-training. Earlier unlearning methods tend to cause over-forgetting because they treat the entire input sequence as the target of unlearning, thereby erasing important linguistic knowledge necessary for maintaining model utility. Recent works explore selective unlearning, which focuses on forgetting only certain portions of the input rather than the whole sequence. However, current selective unlearning methods depend heavily on signals obtained from external models or annotations. In this paper, they present a novel model-intrinsic unlearning technique that identifies the most relevant parts to forget at the token level by estimating differences in gradient responses between forget and retain data. These token-level scores are then utilized to identify larger, coherent spans through self-consistency-based generation processes. Since the unlearning targets are determined purely based on the model's internal behavior, the resulting unlearning objective aligns well with the model's internal mechanisms. Extensive experiments on two popular benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive unlearning performance while significantly improving the preservation of retained knowledge.

Social identity is central to health outcomes yet rarely studied in machine learning applications. They investigate how socially sensitive markers like sexual orientation and religious affiliation impact LLM performance in medical QA. Using counterfactuals to manipulate identity characteristics, they find that homophobe cues trigger large declines in accuracy and certainty calibration across models, with compounded effects under intersectional identities. Their findings highlight the dangers of deploying models relying solely on accuracy and confidence scores to make clinical decisions, especially given the risks of inaccurate uncertainty signals for vulnerable populations.

While recent advances in visionlanguage models demonstrate impressive capabilities for discriminative reasoning, little is known about their practical utility for abductive reasoning. To investigate this, they introduce DixitWorld, an agentbased benchmark that operationalizes multimodal abductive reasoning through the boardgame Dixit. Their large-scale experiments reveal a key asymmetry between the roles of story teller and listener: although large models excel at hypothesis selection (75.6% of models achieved 70+ % accuracy), none of them are competent at generating ambiguous but informative hypotheses - a crucial requirement for hypothesis creation. Even when constrained to selecting from a few options, models still struggle to discriminate meaningfully, with the largest model exhibiting just a 2.4-point margin over humans on a standard hypothesis selection benchmark. Extensive scalability, calibration, and sensitivity studies confirm that this asymmetry is structural, persisting even at state-of-the-art model sizes. By highlighting this central bottleneck, DixitWorld underscores the need for architectures that explicitly model intentions and ambiguity in order to advance robust multimodal abductive reasoning. 1

Event relations capture structured dependencies between events, which are crucial for higher-level reasoning in large language models (LLMs). They propose UERLens, an interpretability framework for understanding event relations in LLMs, with the aim of exploring whether LLMs encode event relations in identifiable and relation-sensitive internal features and whether such features play a functional role in understanding event relations and improving model performance. Through a large-scale counterfactual analysis, they identify relation-sensitive features with clear layer-wise structure and demonstrate their functional impact on event relation extraction. Their analysis reveals that event relations are encoded in a structured manner across layers, emerging at intermediate representational stages rather than being tied to surface-level cues. They further show that these features provide informative representations that can be leveraged by simple models, and that the observed patterns generalize across different datasets and model architectures. The code and data are available at 1.

Coreference resolution faces many challenges when applied to real-world texts. Most existing datasets suffer from three limitations: they are mostly devoted to English, contain only short texts, and focus primarily on factual genres. They overcome these limitations by introducing a multilingual corpus containing over 800 thousand tokens of fanfiction in seven languages. Their corpus includes stories of various lengths and covers a range of genres. All characters are annotated, making this the first annotation scheme for character coreference in fiction. They report annotator agreements and baseline results for coreference systems, providing a valuable resource for future research in multilingual coreference resolution and computational literary studies.

While large language models (LLMs) exhibit great potential for multilingual processing, most LLMs remain focused on English and perform poorly in resource-poor settings. They address this challenge by proposing novel tuning-free multilingual alignment paradigms based on token perturbation. Their primary contribution is the introduction of two methods: Language-Aware Token Boosting (LATB) and Adaptive Language-Aware Token Boosting (Adaptive-LATB). Experimental evaluations on eight languages confirm that both methods effectively reduce language confusion and maintain summarisation performance. This demonstrates the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of their approach to enhance multilingual capabilities of English-centric LLMs. 1

Test-time alignment techniques offer scalable alternatives to training-time fine-tuning approaches for improving large language models (LLM)s performance and safety. Recently, representation-editing-based methods such as RE-Con-trol have emerged as promising test-time alignment solutions. While RE-Control demonstrates impressive alignment capabilities, it does not account for the preference-based nature of most alignment tasks. They propose Pref-CTRL, a novel method that enhances RE-Control with loss functions informed by preference comparisons. Their experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over RE-Control on standard datasets, and comparable performance with a training-time baseline on new datasets.

Most humor datasets focus on popular forms of humor like puns, one-line jokes, and satirical headlines. In contrast, this paper presents a novel dataset consisting of sentences that are deliberately bad - entries from the annual Bulwer-Lytton Fiction Contest, whose purpose is to reward poor writing. Their initial analysis finds that these sentences are fundamentally different from other humor datasets in three ways: (1) they are longer and contain more elements that contribute to the sense of humor; (2) they make greater use of literary devices such as metaphor, metafiction, and alliteration; and (3) they include many more semantically deviant adjective-noun combinations. Further experiments suggest that LLMs can replicate the form of Bulwer-Lytton sentences, but exaggerate their humorous effects.

Chatbots equipped with advanced memory and empathy features are hailed as ideal companions capable of adapting to our needs and providing nuanced emotional counsel. But what happens when they tailor care based on memories shaped by the biases of individual users? Their study shows that the emotional reasoning abilities of large language models are heavily influenced by user profiles, resulting in disparate performance across demographics. A wealthy and influential user is less likely to receive effective emotional guidance than someone struggling to meet basic needs due to systemic disadvantages. They call this phenomenon the "personalisation trap".

As human-agent interaction moves beyond simple conversation tasks toward longterm, socially rich relationships, agents must evolve from static chatbots to dynamic, personalizable personas that adapt to shifting contexts. However, the state-of-the-art techniques for training large-scale language models, including promptengineering and supervised finetuning (SFT), suffer from significant generalization issues in these complex environments due to myopic decision making, error propagation, and rigid personality adherence. They propose a novel Neurosymbolic Agentic Reinforcement Learning (NSARL) framework for OC companionship agents that bridges this generalization gap through a principled approach to policy optimization. Their hybrid framework decomposes the agent's cognitive architecture into three modular sub-policies - Routing, Memory, and Persona -, each of which learns trajectorylevel policies guided by verifiable rewards. Through decomposition, the agent implicitly acquires forward-looking value functions that lead to robust long-horizon planning and memory management. Preliminary evaluations show that NSARL achieves 100% plan recall and improved 46% memory accuracy over baseline models, while demonstrating strong retention of persona consistency despite hallucinations. These early results highlight the need for multiple training paradigms to address the diverse requirements of OC systems.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) offers a powerful framework for refining pre-trained large language models in complex reasoning scenarios. However, it struggles with finding the right balance between exploration and exploitation, a challenge that could compromise its potential benefits. In particular, they find that extreme tokencovariance values disproportionately dominate policy gradient updates, causing entropy instability and ultimately degrading model performance. They propose a GRPO variant that softens extreme covariance contributions via Gaussian kernel reweighting, thus enabling more optimal trade-offs between exploration and exploitation. Extensive experimentation on various mathematical benchmarking tasks demonstrates that their approach yields superior performance compared to vanilla GRPO.

Language models require training steps (especially alignment) that are expensive to perform, time-consuming, and scale poorly with the model size. As such, test-time alignment has become increasingly popular as an alternative. One particular approach is to use a proxy-aligned model, which can be much smaller. Existing work fall into two categories: (i) ones that rely on explicit reward signals extracted from the proxy-aligned model to emulate the distribution of the large base model (Mitchell et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025); and (ii) ones that rely solely on the base model's output while using the proxy model as a fallback option (Fei et al., 2025; Hammal et al., 2026). In this work, they introduce a rejection-based formulation for the proxy-based test-time alignment that covers both classes of solutions and provides a unified view of existing work. More importantly, they propose a new rejection criterion that takes advantage of additional information from the proxy model to assess the confidence of the base model, avoiding reliance on confidence measures that are not motivated. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of their proposal.

While incorporating knowledge graphs enables large language models to perform multi-hop reasoning, they open up a new vulnerability against knowledge poisoning attacks that corrupt the structure of the retrieved graph. They propose HoG-GRAG, a novel defense mechanism that detects poisoning through structural analysis of retrieved subgraphs and repairs potential damage prior to answer generation. Empirically, their method reliably identifies poisoned structures and effectively suppresses them, achieving robust recovery on multi-hop question answering data. Their code is publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/hog-grag.

Text-to-SQL is essential for unlocking enterprise analytics. Previous approaches either rely on general-purpose LLMs or employ advanced agentic frameworks. Both approaches generally suffer from a latency-performance trade-off. They address this challenge by re-framing the task as a software testing paradigm, in which the semantic content of the input question is decomposed into a suite of semantically distinct test cases to be validated against the database. Their parallel exploration paradigm naturally supports parallel execution, planning, and multi-path search, leading to fast and reliable information gathering and efficient semantic searching. To operationalize this paradigm, they develop PEXA, an agent consisting of a Planner, Test Case Generator, and SQL Proposer sub-agents that work together with a shared SQL executor tool. When tested on Spider 2.0, PEXA achieves stateoftheart results while maintaining competitive walltime.

They present a new skill-centric framework for efficient and transparent distillation of reasoning capacity from large-to-small scale. They exploit the hierarchical nature of skills to prioritize training examples that target the student model's weaknesses, and provide skill chains embedded in the data to encourage model awareness of the skill landscape. Their approach improves over baseline methods by +3.0 absolute accuracy across five math benchmarks when using just 1k distillation examples from a 100K corpus.

Can large language models predict scientific feasibility based solely on prior knowledge, or do they benefit from structured experimental evidence? They investigate this question via a novel controlled-evidence framework that isolates how feasibility judgments respond to hypothesis-only input, hypothesis plus experiments, hypothesis plus outcomes, or hypothesis plus experiments and outcomes. Their findings reveal three major challenges: (a) hypothesis-only baselines are surprisingly strong for current models, implying that feasibility assessments must go beyond surface-level alignment; (b) hypothesis-plus-outcome evidence is more stable than hypothesis-plus-experiment evidence; and (c) partial evidence can actively mislead models, causing non-monotonic degradation. These results highlight the importance of diagnostic evaluations and the development of evidence-gated reasoning mechanisms when applying language models to science. 1

Annotation methods for computing-intensive, subjective social phenomena are constrained by scalability, quality, and cost. Increasingly, Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising solution, yet existing approaches typically entail a fundamental tradeoff between quality and deployability. They present a novel LLM-enabled annotation pipeline that introduces light-weight, context-aware dynamic batching mechanisms that adjust batch sizes in real time to reduce inference costs significantly while maintaining interpretive richness crucial to precise annotation. Their evaluation focuses on detecting parasocial interactions in live streams, a complex phenomenon requiring delicate cues, and demonstrates that the proposed pipeline produces competitive performance compared to existing methods, while drastically reducing latency and costs. Implementation details and code are publicly available at https://github.com/fatimahe/CaBSALLM.

Although there is growing interest in studying the faithfulness of reasoning in large language models (LLMs), there remains little consensus on how to interpret and validate the LLM's reasoning process. In this paper, they go beyond previous works that challenge the existence of chain-of-thoughts reasoning. Instead, they reveal that the LLM can introduce spurious biases through semantically unrelated tokens, which can influence both the language generation in the same prompt and other prompts. Their finding calls into question interpretations of the LLM's reasoning process as an explicit chain of logical steps, suggesting that the faithfulness of the LLM's reasoning needs to be re-examined from a different perspective.

They introduce a simple yet effective way to enhance the accuracy of one-step text generation through flowmatching. Inspired by the success of shortcut models in computer vision, they design a new type of flow-matching model that learns to skip steps along the denoising trajectory. By doing so, the model requires fewer denoising iterations, enabling fast inference while maintaining high text quality. Their experiments show that the proposed shortcuts lead to consistent improvements on three widely-used text generation benchmarks.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) plays a pivotal role in the training workflow of Large Language Models (LLM). The standard Cross-Entropy loss function in SFT excessively pulls prediction probabilities towards the true labels, thereby suppressing diversity and increasing the risk of mode collapse. They explore the disparities within the token-level exploration space and propose SED-SFT, a simple yet effective method to selectively promote diversity. It includes a concise entropy regulation term and a masking strategy that prevents excessive diversity enhancement in areas with constrained exploration spaces. Their experiments on eight rigorous mathematical benchmarks using two popular backbone models demonstrate that SED-SFT consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average gain of 2.06% in pass rates after reinforcement learning.

They investigate ways to augment Large Language Models (LLM) with Frame Semantics knowledge. They synthetically construct QA-style supervision over the full FrameNet inventory (1,200+ frames), including constraints on roles, semantics, and frame relations, and use it to train a LoRA extension of Meta-Llama-3. Their goal is to improve event-level representation and reasoning. They use Natural Language Inference (NLI) as a diagnostic to demonstrate that the injected knowledge leads to improved inference, especially for cases requiring frame compatibility, polysemous resolution, and inter-frame relations. This indicates that frame-semantics guided injection extends beyond simple role tagging to enable robust event-level reasoning.

Language models have been found to leak private text during inference, raising concerns about privacy in privacy-sensitive applications. While prior work largely focussed on centralised learning settings, recent efforts have attempted to apply techniques to federated learning environments. However, the current body of literature lacks a systematic exploration of memorisation in federated learning scenarios. In this work, they present a framework that quantifies memorisation across all clients in a federated learning environment. By extending prior work on centralised learning, they develop a pairwise-based metric to measure memorisation over cross-samples and demonstrate its applicability to cross-clients' scenarios. Using this framework, they conduct a series of studies to characterise the memorisation phenomenon and the relevant factors involved. Their results reveal that memorisation does indeed occur in federated learning settings, though intraclass memorisation is consistently larger than interclass memorisation. Furthermore, memorisation is influenced by prefix length, decoding strategy and federated algorithm, highlighting the importance of considering these variables in future research.

While they remain central to natural language expression, metaphor, metonymy, and simile are notoriously difficult to detect due to their intertwined ambiguities and divergent cognitive origins. They tackle this challenge by formulating them as a unified four-class classification task, introducing FL-MSCL: a novel framework that integrates prompt-enhanced representations with supervised contrastive learning. Comprehensive testing demonstrates its superiority over state-of-the-art methods and large-scale LLMs. Their code is available at https://github.com/yizhen-zheng999/FL-MSCL.

They present LRM²QAS – a novel, language-robust, multi-aspect evaluation framework for assessing the quality of generative question answering outputs across resource-limited environments. It combines semantic alignment, question-aware factual coverage, numerical accuracy, and evidence reliability into a unified objective function that facilitates comparative assessment across different dimensions. Experimental results across multiple Indic language benchmarks show that LRM²QAS demonstrates consistently greater alignment with human evaluations than competing metrics. They extend this evaluation to standard open-domain QA datasets and find that it aligns better with human judgments in terms of correctness than embedding-based metrics such as BERTScore. These findings establish a principled foundation for evaluating QA systems and highlight persistent challenges in generating accurate outputs in multilingual settings.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated great potential in improving the quality of text-to-speech (TTS) systems. Recently, preference optimization techniques have been employed to enhance intelligibility and naturalness in the TTS system. However, current methods require paired data consisting of desirable and undesirable outputs for the same utterance, which is rarely available due to imbalanced distribution and costly human annotations, thereby causing significant data inefficiency. Additionally, since preference alignment is performed at the utterance level while the actual task involves optimizing at the token level, there is a misalignment issue. To resolve these problems, they propose Token-level Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (TKTO), a new preference optimization technique that quantifies token-level importance and conducts preference alignment at the token level. Their experiments show that TKTO significantly improves the performance over the state-of-the-art systems, reducing the character error rate by 54% in the Japanese language and achieving an accuracy of 0.958. Due to its data-efficiency, TKTO can utilize 6× more training data than the existing DPO-based preference optimization methods. Moreover, it automatically provides 12.8× stronger rewards to desired tokens.

Image inpainting, a popular paradigm for reconstructing visual inputs to feed into language models, can introduce subtle but semantically disruptive artifacts. While modern inpainting models strive for pixel-level realism, they often fail to address more subtle semantic deviations that lead to object substitutions or attribute changes in downstream captions. To study this relationship, they introduce a two-stage diagnostic framework where inpainted images are passed to language models for analysis. Through systematic analysis across multiple datasets, they find strong correlations between reconstruction fidelity and linguistic grounding, with higher perceptual fidelity leading to stronger caption accuracy. They further show that inpainting induces layer-dependent attention drift in vision encoders, with semantic instability localized to reconstructed regions. Their findings indicate that inpainting can alter downstream language behavior and motivate reconstruction-aware diagnostics when evaluating vision-language robustness.

Large language models demonstrate surprising commonsense reasoning abilities, but existing benchmarks restrict evaluation to singleatomic predictions. In reality, common-sense problems often admit multiple plausible interpretations, yet most benchmarks treat them as competing atomic alternatives. They address this gap by introducing LOGICAL -COM-MONSENSEQA, a benchmark that frames commonsense reasoning as logical composition over multiple plausible answers. Using symbolic operations to represent joint plausibility, partial plausibility, and joint implausibility, LOGICAL -COMMONSENSEQA enables explicit testing of compositional, multi-answer reasoning. Experiments reveal that although LLMs perform reasonably well on conjunctive reasoning and moderately on disjunctive reasoning, they fail sharply on negation-based reasoning, highlighting persistent challenges in compositional commonsense reasoning.

They present BioHiCL, a new dense retriever tailored for biological applications, which utilizes hierarchical MeSH annotation supervision to capture fine-grained semantic overlaps between texts. Unlike traditional retrieval tasks that rely on coarse-grained binary relevance or instance-level signals, MeSH offers granular, multi-aspect supervision by annotating document-level concepts with hierarchical categories reflecting multiple levels of specificity. They design a contrastive learning objective that aligns embedding similarity with depth-aware MeSH label similarity, enabling the model to learn about semantic overlap within MeSH subgraphs. Through simple LoRA fine-tuning, they transfer a generic-domain dense retriever to the biomedical domain via hierarchical MeSH supervision, outperforming state-of-the-art methods across several benchmark tests. Their approach also demonstrates high computational efficiency on standard hardware.

Dialogue is central to building intelligent teams. In multi-agency environments, the complexity grows due to ambiguities, conflicting interests, and rapidly changing circumstances. Recent advances in large language models offer exciting opportunities, but existing multi-agent systems remain fragile when confronted with the realities of cooperative human-machine or machine-human interactions. They identify weaknesses in current architectures and evaluation strategies, showing how classical dialogical theories can guide the design of robust and transparent agentic systems. Dialogues are not just interfaces separating planning from action, but are essential for managing joint activities. Their recommendations include: 1) Treating dialogue as a planning component to address ambiguity proactively; 2) Evaluating the quality of dialogue behaviors even when final outputs appear satisfactory; 3) Modeling memory and perception as socially constructed states; 4) Implementing negotiation protocols to resolve reference mismatches. Through these principles, designers can build agentic systems that prioritize cooperation, and policymakers can ensure that the consequences of dialogue are measured.

Modern Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation approaches aim to retrieve the most relevant code outside individual files to feed into large-scale language models. However, semantic loss due to inadequate chunking often hinders the generation quality. They propose Late Code Chunking (LC 2 ), a retrieval-aware strategy that provides expanded and augmented retrieved code segments to mitigate semantic loss. Their method creates two contexts: (1) Code Retrieval Context, focusing on effective retrieval of related content, and (2) Code Comprehension Context, restoring missing semantic elements through expansion and augmentation of retrieved code. Experiments on two benchmarks show consistent improvements across different large-scale language models.

Recent work suggests that large language models can achieve near-human forecasting performance, prompting interest in assessing their capabilities rapidly via retrospection. To enable fast testing, forecasts are made based on retrieved documents from the web, and search-engine date filters are commonly employed to restrict retrieved content to information available at the moment of forecasting. They investigate whether datefiltered searches actually succeed in blocking information leakage during retroactive forecasting. By auditing Google Search's before: filter and DuckDuckGo's date range filter, they discover widespread leakage - at least one page with major post-cut-off information appears on 71% of questions on Google and 81% on DuckDuckGo. Even worse, the answer is directly revealed on 41% of questions on Google and 55% on DuckDuckGo. They link this leakage to multiple mechanisms, ranging from updated content and related article sections to absence-based signals and unreliable metadata. Their findings show that date-restricted search alone cannot yield credible evaluation, calling for stronger retrieval protections or evaluation on frozen, timestamped web snapshots.

They explore how the notion of problem difficulty is represented and generalized in large multilingual models. By analyzing 21 languages of mathematics problems, they find that difficulty is represented in a depth-dependent manner. An early, shallow representation enables strong cross-lingual generalization, supporting a shared, language-independent representation of difficulty. In contrast, deeper layers refine this signal into a language-specific form, improving monolingual accuracy but reducing cross-lingual alignment. Their analysis highlights the potential for multilingual applications to benefit from a common representation of difficulty, formed before language-specific reasoning begins.

Masked diffusion models offer an alternative to autoregressive decoding, allowing for parallel generation of longer sequences. They propose a simple strategy to gradually increase block size, preserving reasoning capabilities seen in smallblock diffusion models.

Listwise reranking has emerged as a promising paradigm for leveraging Large Language Models to rank entire document sets in parallel. However, it encounters a fundamental limitation: positional sensitivity leads to systematic degradation in ranking accuracy. Current approaches to address this issue either impose unacceptable delays (through inference-time aggregation) or require costly re-training (through data augmentation/architecture design), thereby limiting flexibility. They propose CapCal, a simple yet effective training-free framework that removes position bias from ranking decisions at inference time. Specifically, they quantify the content-agnostic prior by querying the model with empty placeholders and perform contrastive calibration to isolate the positional bias from the ranking distribution. Experimental results on ten benchmark tasks demonstrate that CapCal preserves single-pass efficiency while improving ranking performance, providing gains 10× higher than those achieved by large models on tasks with extreme positional bias. Through ablation studies, they show how their calibration strategy achieves competitive ranking performance even with compact models, narrowing the performance gap between small and large models in listwise reranking.

Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) for specific downstream tasks presents two fundamental challenges: 1) achieving robust generalization across diverse tasks without compromising LLM's original architecture, and 2) performing fast adaptation with limited data given potential differences between pre-trained and fine-tuned representations. Recent advances in metalearning offer a solution by learning generalized, task-adaptive parameters during meta-training. However, existing metalearning formulations either jointly optimize generalization and adaptation under conflicting goals (Finn et al., 2017; Sinha et al., 2024) or restrict adaptation to gradient-based procedures that may be unsuitable for heterogenous tasks (Zhang et al., 2025b). To resolve these issues, they introduce a decoupled metalearning formulation that separates parameter exploration for generalization from parameter adjustment for task adaptation. Specifically, they meta-learn a task-conditioned parameter generator to explore a shared parameter space across tasks, and perform iterative, task-specific adjustments via closed-loop reinforcement learning after generating initial parameter adaptations. Their decoupling enables flexible adaptation strategies tailored to each task, avoiding premature convergence to suboptimal adaptation trajectories. They validate this formulation on a variety of benchmark tasks and find that their method consistently improves performance relative to strong metalearning and multi-task baselines.

AI research is challenging to replicate and reuse because its knowledge is implicitly encoded within complex pipelines of interdependent methods, codebases, and configuration parameters. They tackle this issue through Executable Knowledge Graphs (XKG), a novel paper-centric knowledge base that externally represents scientific knowledge in a verifiable and executable format. By grounding abstract academic concepts in concrete code, XKG provides agents with guidance during highlevel planning and lowlevel execution, improving their ability to read, replicate, and reuse AI research. Extensive experiments show consistent improvements in three different agent frameworks across various models. Their XKG is fully automated and evolves alongside recent developments in AI research. 1

Recent advances in multilingual language models enable large-scale reasoning through reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning. State-of-the-art multimodal reasoning models (MRMs) trained for specific tasks (e.g. mathematics) demonstrate impressive abilities to perform step-by-step reasoning. They investigate whether such reasoning techniques transfer to spatial tasks requiring rich perception and holistic reasoning about geometry. Across nineteen models evaluated on thirteen benchmarks, they discover that reasoning models typically underperform their base models on spatial tasks. Moreover, CoT prompting degrades performance by an average of 3% across a wide variety of models. Their analysis reveals that this decline is due to hallucinations caused by text-based reasoning chains, especially when prompted with empty images and "Cannot determine" options. This work emphasizes the importance of designing reasoning frameworks that support human-like vision processing without reliance on hallucinated imagery. Code and pre-trained models are publicly available at github.com/microsoft/CoT-degrades-VSR.

Diffusion models provide a natural platform for iterative denoising, making them appealing for Named Entity Recognition tasks. However, empirical evidence suggests that in practice, the multi-step refinement process is rarely leveraged when trained with exponential moving average. They propose an Initializer-Restorer framework that begins diffusion processing with entities identified by a pretrained model, enabling the multi-step process to refine these candidates. Their method outperforms a competitive diffusion-based NER system and enables multi-step refinement on three standard benchmarks.

Natural language masking techniques have proven effective in learning protein representations through selfsupervision. Despite their versatility, these approaches tend to overlook centuries-old biological interpretations encoded in textual form. They introduce ProteinSTORY, a multi-stage representation learner that synthesizes multiple, heterogenous text sources to create a coherent semantic signature of the protein's biological story. Their model compresses complex narratives about protein families, structural motifs, and cellular localization into a single embedding, achieving better performance in both retrieval and downstream tasks. Most importantly, it bridges the gap between natural language and proteins, enabling text-driven protein search.

Autoregressive (AR) language models have long been popular, despite criticisms regarding issues like exposure bias. Non-autoregressive (NAR) models have emerged as a promising alternative, owing to their ability to make independent predictions and hence allow for fast parallel decoding. Though some initial success was achieved with NAR models in controlled-text-generation tasks, there is still a lack of understanding of how NAR models behave under search-based decoders. In this work, they study the decoding space of NAR models through lexically constrained text generation. Specifically, they propose a novel search-based decoder called LexMAP based on the Directed Acyclic Transformer (DAT). Experimental results indicate that LexMAP achieves full constraint coverage and competitive BLEU score, but lower neuralmetric scores than autoregressive models with Grid Beam Search (GBS). More importantly, they analyze the decoding space of DAT-based NAR models and uncover several interesting characteristics, including reduced MAP degradation, less positional bias, and higher accumulated beam probabilities under the DAT distribution. These findings offer valuable insights into the behavior of NAR models and point to promising directions for future research.

مع تزايد شعبية النماذج اللغوية الكبيرة (LLMs)، أصبحت أدوات تعديلها الموجهة للمعاينة فعالة للغاية بشكل متزايد لإجراء التعديل الدقيق على هذه النماذج. ومن بين الأساليب الحديثة، تعد طريقة التعديل الدقيق القائمة على التمثيلات (ReFT) خيارًا غير تقليدي لتعظيم كفاءة استخدام المعاملات. لكن، لا تزال الطرق الحالية للتعديل القائم على التمثيلات تعتمد بشكل أساسي على تمثيلات ثابتة ومحددة مسبقًا، مما يؤدي إلى أداء غير مرضٍ. مستوحين من دراساتهم حول آليات التركيز في LLMs، حددوا أهمية علامات الفاصلة، التي تُعد نقاط توجيه دلالية مهمة للغاية. لذلك، اقترحوا طريقة “التدرج الدقيق القائم على العلامات الفصلية” (PuReFT)، وهي طريقة جديدة لتعديل التمثيلات عبر تعديل تمثيلات علامات الفاصلة. وبفضل دورها الواضح كنقاط توجيه دلالية، فإن PuReFT توفر قدرة تناسب أفضل مع سلاسل الأحرف الطويلة. وقد أجروا تجارب واسعة باستخدام مجموعة بيانات مختلفة مثل العمليات الرياضية والتفكير السليم وإنشاء الرموز البرمجية، وأظهروا أن PuReFT يمكنه تحقيق أداء ممتاز، سواء بالمقارنة مع طرق تعديل المعاملات التقليدية مثل LoRA، أو بأداء مماثل لتلك الطرق القائمة على التمثيلات الأخرى مثل ReFT. كما أنه يحافظ على معدل زيادة عدد المعاملات المرتفعة إلى حد كبير، وهو ما يجعله الخيار الأمثل لتعديل LLMs في عمليات التطبيقات المختلفة.

أصبحت طريقة تحفيز السلوك عن طريق سلاسل الحجج (Chain-of-Thought Prompting)، التي تستفيد بشكل أساسي من المنطق الرياضي، القيمة المطلقة في التحسينات الأخيرة على نماذج اللغة الكبيرة. وقد أثبت أن الاستدلال الذاتي (Self-Consistency)، وهو طريقة تعتمد على استخدام عدة سلوكيات للتفكير ضمن إطار إجراءات Chain-of-Thought Prompting، يحسّن الأداء على مجموعة من الاختبارات تتطلب منطق رمزي بسيط مثل “كم عدد ضوئيات الشمس؟”. لكن حتى الآن لم يتم دراسة فعالية هذه الطريقة في تسجيل المعرفة الواسعة كجزء من عملية الإجابة على الأسئلة. ولحل هذا الفراغ البحثي، قاموا بتقسيم مجموعة البيانات المعيارية الموسومة بـ MMLU باستخدام تقنية هياكلية قائمة على معاملات سابقة؛ وأظهر تقييمهم أن الاستدلال الذاتي يؤدي إلى تحسن مستمر في الأداء، سواء بالنسبة للمهام المتعلقة بالمنطق الرمزي أم تسجيل المعرفة الواسعة، رغم أن الأساس هو افتراضها الأولي بأن الاستدلال الذاتي لا يؤثر على الأداء في تسجيل المعرفة الواسعة. وبفضل ذلك، حققوا دقة بلغت 89% على مجموعة بيانات MMLU، وهي أعلى دقة تم تحقيقها حتى الآن باستخدام نموذج GPT-4o. ويعتقدون أن هذا العمل قد يكون حافزاً جيداً لإجراء المزيد من التجارب حول تصنيف المهام بدقة أكبر، مما سيكشف المزيد عن كيفية عمل نماذج اللغة الكبيرة.

تقدم طرقهم لتحسين قدرات نماذج اللغة الكبيرة على التفكير البصري، وذلك عن طريق إدخال رسوم بيانية اصطناعية بفعالية مع الحفاظ على الأداء في المهام اللغوية الأساسية. تميز طريقة LAMI بشكل أساسي في اعتمادها على (أ) بنية دمج متاخرة، حيث يتم دمج الخصائص البصرية مع تمثيلات اللغة في المرحلة الأخيرة من عملية التنبؤ، و(ب) استخدام عدة رسم بياني أثناء عمليات الاستدلال، بدلاً من الاعتماد على رسم واحد كما هو الحال في الأساليب السابقة. يوفر هذا الإجراء طرقاً أكثر فعالية للوصول إلى المعلومات البصرية، كما أن تصحيحات التنبؤات التي يقدمها الرسوم البيانية المتعددة غالبًا ما تكون مبنية على أساس صحي. وتُظهر التجارب الشاملة أن LAMI يؤدي بشكل جيد في مجالات الفهم البصري والتفكير حول الكائنات، وهو أقوى بكثير من الأساليب السابقة المستخدمة لتزويد نماذج اللغة بالمعطيات البصرية، مع تحقيق تحسن مماثل لأداء نماذج الذكاء البصري والمعلوماتية المتعددة الوسائط، مع وجود زيادة خفيفة في الوقت الذي يستغرقه عملية الاستدلال. وأخيرًا، عندما تطبق هذه الطريقة على نموذج Llama-3، فإنها تحسّن الأداء عند التعامل مع النصوص فقط بينما لا تزيد من وقت المعالجة. يمكن الحصول على الكود ومجموعات البيانات عبر الرابط التالي: https://github.com/GAI-ASU/LAMI.  
النص المدخل: كيف تتغير حجم الجملة؟  
الرسوم البيانية المولدة: [رجل يرفع كتلة كبيرة].  
التنبؤات بعد الدمج: (رجل يحمل كيس كبير – كيس كبير).  
النتيجة النهائية: كيس كبير.  

النص المدخل: ما هي الحالة الحالية لمونديفيكيو؟  
الرسوم البيانية المولدة: [متاحف تحتوي على دراجات نارية، جزء من حديقة بمونديفيكو].  
التنبؤات بعد الدمج: (متحف، حديقة بمونديفيكو – حديقة بمونديفيكو).  
النتيجة النهائية: حديقة بمونديفيكو.

تقدم طرقية جديدة لأداء المهام متعددة الخطوات في الحوار البشري المتعدد الجوانب، وهي “FULL DUPLEX-BENCH-V2”. يوفر هذا الإطار تجارب حوارية واقعية باللغة المنطوقة باستخدام زوج من أنظمة التحدث، مع قدرة على التعامل مع التغييرات المستمرة في السياق والتدخلات العشوائية بين الأطراف المشاركة. تتكون هذه الطرقية من مُختبر ذكي يقوم بتقييم سلاسة عملية بناء الجمل، ومدى تطبيق التعليمات المتعددة الخطوات، بالإضافة إلى معايير محددة لكل مهمة ضمن أربع فئات مختلفة هي: الحياة اليومية، والإصلاحات، تتبع الكيانات، والأمان. كما يمكن استخدامها كبيئة اختبار موحدة لتقييم الوكلاء الذين يستخدمون تقنية التحدث على مستوى الرموز بشكل مستمر. وتؤكد دراسة شاملة للتقييم البشرية توافقاً متوسطاً إلى قوياً بين القضاة الآليين والمعلقات البشرية، مما يثبت صحة هذه الطريقة للإجابة على أسئلة حول الحوار البشري المتعدد الجوانب عبر الإنترنت.
